segments.narration: Ancient stone forts across Scotland were mysteriously melted into glass. Explorers were baffled by Iron Age ruins where massive granite boulders fused together like volcanic rock.
Melting granite requires temperatures over eleven hundred degrees Celsius—heat typical of a modern blast furnace.
How did prehistoric tribes generate industrial infernos on freezing, wind-swept hilltops?
While early antiquarians imagined ancient superweapons, archaeologists found these fort ramparts were built with dense internal timber frameworks.
While experimental archaeologists tried to recreate the intense heat using bonfires and stone piles, exactly how these massive structures were vitrified remains a subject of ongoing debate.

accuracy_flags.claim: Experiments demonstrated that burning the timber framework in strong winds creates a furnace effect capable of melting the stone.
accuracy_flags.note: The reference mentions that past experiments (such as by Childe and Thornycroft / Ian Ralston) produced only a few partially vitrified stones and that no clear answers were gleaned as to how large-scale forts could actually be crafted this way.

verdicts.claim: Dozens of Iron Age hillforts in Scotland feature stone walls that were melted into glass.
verdicts.note: The reference notes over 70 vitrified fort examples in Scotland spanning Iron Age and early medieval periods, featuring fusion/glassy enamel-like coating on rocks.

verdicts.claim: Melting granite requires temperatures exceeding 1,100 degrees Celsius.
verdicts.note: The reference articles mention the application of intense heat and fusion of rocks, but do not state a specific temperature like 1,100 degrees Celsius.

verdicts.claim: Archaeologists discovered that vitrified fort ramparts were constructed with internal timber frameworks.
verdicts.note: The reference text discusses vitrification caused by intense heat and carefully maintained fires, as well as experiments with piles of stones and bonfires, but does not mention internal timber frameworks.

verdicts.claim: Experiments demonstrated that burning the timber framework in strong winds creates a furnace effect capable of melting the stone.
verdicts.note: The reference mentions that past experiments (such as by Childe and Thornycroft / Ian Ralston) produced only a few partially vitrified stones and that no clear answers were gleaned as to how large-scale forts could actually be crafted this way.
